# Summary of the Green Party Manifesto 2024

## Overview and Context

The Green Party manifesto addresses what it identifies as major challenges facing the UK: a cost of living crisis, strained public services, housing shortages, and climate change. The document outlines policies across healthcare, housing, energy, economy, welfare, environment, education, transport, and international affairs.

## Healthcare and Social Care

The manifesto proposes £28bn additional annual NHS spending by 2030, plus £20bn capital investment over five years. Key commitments include reducing waiting lists, guaranteeing GP access, ensuring NHS dentist availability for all, boosting staff pay, and opposing privatisation. For social care, the party proposes free personal care, increased carer pay, and £20bn annual investment. Mental health services would receive parity with physical health, with 28-day maximum waits for therapy.

## Housing

The manifesto commits to 150,000 new social homes annually, ending right-to-buy, empowering councils to introduce rent controls, ending no-fault evictions, and a major home insulation programme. Investment of £29bn over five years would retrofit homes, with additional funding for heating systems and climate adaptation.

## Energy and Environment

The party proposes wind power providing 70% of UK electricity by 2030, no new oil and gas licences, ending fossil fuel subsidies, and community ownership of energy infrastructure. A carbon tax starting at £120 per tonne would be introduced. Water companies would be renationalised. Environmental measures include a Rights of Nature Act, 30% of land and seas protected by 2030, and strengthened pollution enforcement.

## Economy and Work

Average annual investment of £40bn is proposed for green economic transformation, including electricity infrastructure, building retrofits, railways, and public transport. Railways and water companies would return to public ownership. A £15 minimum wage for all ages, maximum 10:1 pay ratios, and strengthened union rights are proposed. Support for SMEs would include regional mutual banks and grants for decarbonisation.

## Welfare and Public Finances

Universal Credit would increase by £40 weekly, the two-child benefit cap would be abolished, disability benefits would rise 5%, and the five-week benefit wait would end. Funding would come from wealth taxes (1% on assets above £10m, 2% above £1bn), aligned capital gains tax rates, reformed inheritance tax, and carbon taxation. The party estimates raising £50-70bn annually from tax reforms.

## Education

Proposals include £8bn school investment with £2bn for teacher pay, £2.5bn annually for building repairs, £5bn for SEND provision, and £12bn for skills and further education. Tuition fees would be scrapped and maintenance grants restored. Academies would return to local authority control.

## Transport

£10bn annual subsidies for rail and buses are proposed, with free bus travel for under-18s. Railways would be renationalised. £2.5bn annually would fund cycleways and footpaths. Petrol and diesel vehicle sales would end by 2027, with a scrappage scheme for electric vehicle transition. A frequent-flyer levy and ban on short domestic flights are proposed.

## Democracy and Migration

The manifesto proposes replacing first-past-the-post with proportional representation, votes at 16, an elected second chamber replacing the Lords, and a constitutional commission. Migration policy would end the hostile environment, create safe asylum routes, permit asylum seekers to work, and remove minimum income requirements for family visas.

## International Affairs

The party supports an immediate bilateral ceasefire in Gaza, Palestinian state recognition, ending UK arms exports to Israel, and investigating war crimes. Overseas aid would rise to 1% of GNI by 2033. The party supports EU membership rejoining when feasible, signing the UN nuclear weapons prohibition treaty, cancelling Trident, and reforming NATO towards diplomacy and dialogue.

## Funding

Total additional spending by 2030 would reach approximately £160bn revenue and £90bn capital annually, funded through personal and wealth taxes (£73bn), business taxes (£8bn), carbon taxes (£91bn), and borrowing.
